source_text: Superest ad concludendam materiolam de observatione quoque dandi et accipiendi Baptismum commonefacere. Dandi quidem habet jus summus sacerdos, qui est episcopus. Dehinc presbyteri et diaconi, non tamen sine episcopi auctoritate, propter Ecclesiae honorem. Quo salvo, salva pax est. Alioquin etiam laicis jus est. Quod enim ex aequo accipitur, ex aequo dari potest, nisi episcopi jam aut presbyteri, aut diaconi vocantur, discentes, Domini sermo non debet abscondi ab ullo. Proinde et Baptismus aeque Dei census ab omnibus exerceri potest: sed quanto magis laicis disciplina verecundiae et modestiae incumbit, cum ea majoribus competat, ne sibi assumant dicatum episcopi officium episcopatus. Aemulatio schismatum mater est. Omnia licere, dixit sanctissimus Apostolus, sed non omnia expedire. Sufficiat scilicet in necessitatibus ut utaris, sicubi aut loci, aut temporis, aut personae conditio compellit. Tunc enim constantia succurrentis excipitur, cum urget circumstantia periclitantis. Quoniam reus erit perditi hominis, si supersederit praestare, quod libere potuit. Petulantia autem mulieris quae usurpavit docere, utique non etiam tinguendi jus sibi pariet, nisi si quae nova bestia evenerit similis pristinae: ut quemadmodum illa Baptismum auferebat, ita aliqua per se eum conferat. Quod si quae Paulo perperam adscripta sunt, exemplum Theclae ad licentiam mulierum docendi tinguendique defendunt; sciant in Asia presbyterum, qui eam scripturam construxit, quasi titulo Pauli de suo cumulans, convictum atque confessum id se amore Pauli fecisse, loco decessisse. Quam enim fidei proximum videretur, ut is docendi et tinguendi daret foeminae potestatem, qui ne discere quidem constanter mulieri permisit: Taceant, et domi maritos suos consulant.
pass_a_gloss: It remains to conclude the material by also warning about the observation of giving and receiving Baptism. Indeed, the highest priest, who is the bishop, has the right of giving. Next, presbyters and deacons, yet not without the bishop's authority, on account of the honor of the Church. With this preserved, peace is preserved. Otherwise, even laypeople have the right. For what is received equally can be given equally, unless the bishop or presbyters or deacons are already called, learners, the Lord's word ought not to be hidden from anyone. Accordingly, even Baptism can be exercised equally by all as God's judgment: but how much more does the discipline of modesty and reverence incumbent upon laypeople, when these things are suitable for greater ones, lest they assume to themselves the dedicated office of the bishop. Emulation of schisms is the mother. All things are permitted, said the most holy Apostle, but not all things are expedient. It is enough, of course, to use in necessities, wherever either the condition of place or time or person compels. For then the constancy of the one succoring is accepted, when the circumstance of the one in danger urges. For he will be guilty of the loss of a person, if he neglects to provide what he could freely. Moreover, the petulance of the woman who usurped teaching will certainly not also procure for herself the right of baptizing, unless some new beast similar to the former arises: so that just as that one took away Baptism, so some woman confers it by herself. But if some things were wrongly ascribed to Paul, they defend the example of Thecla for the license of women teaching and baptizing; let them know that in Asia a presbyter, who constructed that scripture, piling it up as if with the title of Paul from his own, was convicted and confessed that he did this out of love for Paul, and departed from his position. For what would seem nearest to faith, that he would give the power of teaching and baptizing to a woman, who did not even permit a woman to learn constantly: Let them be silent, and consult their husbands at home.

bible_refs.note: All things are permitted, but not all things are expedient
Let them be silent, and consult their husbands at home

pass_b_english: One last item before we close this material: a warning about who may give and who may receive Baptism. The right to give it belongs first to the high priest — that is, the bishop. Next come presbyters and deacons, but never without the bishop's authorization, for the sake of the Church's honor. Keep that authority intact, and peace stays intact; discard it, and even laypeople claim the right. The logic is blunt: what is received on equal terms can be given on equal terms, provided no bishop, presbyter, or deacon has already been summoned. Learners must not be kept from the Lord's word. (1 Corinthians 6:12) Accordingly, Baptism — God's own assessment — can be exercised by all alike. Yet the discipline of modesty and reverence weighs all the more heavily on laypeople, precisely because those qualities belong to the greater orders, lest layfolk usurp the bishop's consecrated office. Rivalry is the mother of schism. 'All things are permitted,' said the most holy Apostle, 'but not all things are expedient.' In emergencies — when place, time, or the condition of the person forces the issue — it is enough to act. The constancy of the one who steps in is recognized only when the peril of the one in danger demands it; otherwise the helper becomes guilty of that person's loss for failing to give what he freely could.

As for the woman who insolently seized the right to teach, her petulance will certainly not win her the right to baptize either — unless some new beast arises like the primeval one, so that just as that creature took Baptism away, some woman might now confer it on her own. If certain writings falsely attributed to Paul are waved around, citing Thecla's example to license women teaching and baptizing, let them learn the facts: in Asia a presbyter who fabricated that scripture, padding it with Paul's name as if it were his own, was convicted and confessed he did it out of love for Paul, and was stripped of his office. How could it seem consistent with faith that the same apostle who would not even permit a woman to learn steadily — 'Let them be silent, and consult their husbands at home' — would hand her the power to teach and to baptize? (1 Corinthians 14:34-35)

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass A provides a literal rendering, while Pass B provides a fluent English version that preserves all nuances, including the conditional clauses and the historical anecdote regarding the presbyter in Asia. Scripture citations (1 Corinthians 6:12 and 1 Corinthians 14:34-35) correctly identify the source of the quoted/alluded phrases in the Latin text.
